claim: Choices rely on a transformation of sensory inputs into motor responses.
source: Choices rely on a transformation of sensory inputs into motor responses.
evidence: This is a general statement about choice processes that is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The evolution of a choice process has been tracked by projecting population neural responses into state spaces using invasive single neuron recordings.
source: Using invasive single neuron recordings, the evolution of a choice process has been tracked by projecting population neural responses into state spaces.
evidence: This refers to established methods in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The authors developed an approach that allows recovery of similar trajectories on a millisecond timescale in non-invasive human recordings.
source: Here, we develop an approach that allows us to recover similar trajectories on a millisecond timescale in non-invasive human recordings.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors selectively suppress activity related to three task-axes: relevant and irrelevant sensory inputs and response direction in magnetoencephalography data.
source: We selectively suppress activity related to three task-axes, relevant and irrelevant sensory inputs and response direction, in magnetoencephalography data acquired during context-dependent choices.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation used in the study.

claim: Recordings from premotor cortex show a progression from processing sensory input to processing the response.
source: Recordings from premotor cortex show a progression from processing sensory input to processing the response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the MEG data analysis shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In contrast to previous macaque recordings, information related to choice-irrelevant features is represented more weakly than choice-relevant sensory information in human premotor cortex.
source: In contrast to previous macaque recordings, information related to choice-irrelevant features is represented more weakly than choice-relevant sensory information.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing human data to previous NHP studies, supported by the data in Figure 3B.

claim: Humans were trained on over 20,000 trials of the task to test whether extensive over-training changes the mechanistic difference between species.
source: To test whether this mechanistic difference between species is caused by extensive over-training common in non-human primate studies, we trained humans on >20,000 trials of the task.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the training phase.

claim: Choice-irrelevant features were still weaker than relevant features in premotor cortex after over-training.
source: Choice-irrelevant features were still weaker than relevant features in premotor cortex after over-training.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the post-training data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A major shift from looking at individual neurons to studying population responses has begun to shed light on larger-scale neural dynamics.
source: More recently, a major shift from looking at individual neurons to studying population responses has begun to shed light on larger-scale neural dynamics, thus providing insight into previously hidden circuit mechanisms (Cunningham et al., 2014; Yuste, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Population activity is projected into neural state space by defining the major axes of variation of a neural population.
source: Usually, in this approach, the major axes of variation of a neural population are defined and the population activity is projected into this neural state space.
evidence: This describes an established method in neuroscience.

claim: Population response analysis has begun to revolutionize understanding of the evolution of choice in parietal and frontal cortices.
source: This new way of looking at neural firing rates has begun to revolutionize our understanding of various neural processes, including the evolution of choice in parietal and frontal cortices (Harvey et al., 2012; Mante et al., 2013; Morcos and Harvey, 2016; Raposo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Population response analysis has provided insights into critical stages of movement preparation and reaching in premotor and motor cortices.
source: the critical stages of movement preparation and reaching in premotor and motor cortices (Churchland et al., 2012; Kaufman et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Population response analysis has provided insights into mechanisms underlying working memory in prefrontal cortex.
source: and the mechanisms underlying working memory in prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Murray et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Deriving neural population trajectories requires invasive recordings because the population vector is constructed from the firing rate of individual neurons.
source: Yet deriving neural population trajectories requires invasive recordings because the population vector is constructed from the firing rate of individual neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current methods, based on established knowledge.

claim: No comparable non-invasive techniques for use in healthy human participants have been established to date for deriving population-like trajectories.
source: As a consequence, to date, no comparable non-invasive techniques for use in healthy human participants have been established.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Repetition suppression takes advantage of a feature first observed over 50 years ago showing that the activity of a neuron will be suppressed when it is repeatedly exposed to features it is sensitive to.
source: Repetition suppression (or 'adaptation') takes advantage of a feature first observed over 50 years ago (Gross et al., 1967), showing that the activity of a neuron will be suppressed when it is repeatedly exposed to features it is sensitive to.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to early work on repetition suppression.

claim: Repetition suppression has been widely replicated and shown to be a robust property of neurons in single-unit recordings.
source: This phenomenon has since been widely replicated and shown to be a robust property of neurons in single-unit recordings (for review, see Barron et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The bulk signal measured from thousands or millions of neurons using EEG, MEG, or fMRI will show suppression if a subset of these neurons is sensitive to a repeated feature.
source: Importantly, the bulk signal measured from thousands or millions of neurons using techniques such as electroencephalography (EEG), MEG, or functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) will also show suppression if a subset of these neurons is sensitive to a repeated feature.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about how repetition suppression manifests in bulk signals.

claim: Repetition suppression provides insight into the activity of specific subpopulations of neurons in non-invasive recordings.
source: Thus, repetition suppression provides insight into the activity of specific subpopulations of neurons in these non-invasive recordings available for use in humans and, in that way, allows us to examine the underlying neural mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of repetition suppression.

claim: PMd is the key region for choosing hand digit responses.
source: PMd is the key region for choosing hand digit responses (Dum and Strick, 2002; Rushworth et al., 2003), the response modality in our choice task.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Repetition suppression provides the best resolution achievable using non-invasive MEG when neural representations of interest are located within one brain region.
source: Given this spatial focus, repetition suppression provides the best resolution achievable using non-invasive MEG: a single sensor or voxel is sufficient to reveal feature-processing using repetition suppression.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the repetition suppression approach.

claim: Multivariate approaches rely on spatial patterns detected across sensors, which would not offer the required spatial scale for studying processes within one brain region.
source: By contrast, multivariate approaches rely on spatial patterns detected across sensors, which would not offer the required spatial scale.
evidence: This is a comparison of methods based on their properties.

claim: The authors extended the repetition suppression framework by suppressing the MEG signal to multiple different features within the same experiment.
source: Here, we extend the repetition suppression framework in one crucial way: we suppress the MEG signal to multiple different features within the same experiment.
evidence: This describes the methodological innovation of the study.

claim: Adaptation along each feature can be conceptualized as 'squashing' the neural response along one task dimension, or task-axis.
source: Adaptation along each feature can be conceptualised as 'squashing' the neural response along one task dimension, or task-axis.
evidence: This is a conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: It is possible to simultaneously induce adaptation along multiple task-axes in non-invasive human recordings using repetition suppression.
source: Our first key result shows that it is possible, using repetition suppression, to simultaneously induce adaptation along multiple task-axes in non-invasive human recordings.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the experimental data.

claim: The recovered human choice traces show a progression from processing of choice inputs to processing of the motor response, just like in invasive recordings from non-human primates.
source: The recovered human choice traces show a progression from a processing of choice inputs to a processing of the motor response, just like in invasive recordings from non-human primates (NHPs) (Mante et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing the results to previous NHP work, supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: A large body of evidence in human and non-human primates shows that selection of relevant sensory inputs occurs through top-down modulations from prefrontal and parietal regions onto early sensory regions.
source: A large body of evidence in human and non-human primates shows that selection of relevant sensory inputs occurs through top-down modulations from prefrontal and parietal regions onto early sensory regions (Buschman and Miller, 2007; de Lange et al., 2010; Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Egner and Hirsch, 2005; Everling et al., 2002; Friston, 2005; Friston and Kiebel, 2009; Gazzaley et al., 2007; Kok et al., 2016; Michalareas et al., 2016; Moore and Zirnsak, 2017; Noudoost et al., 2010; Pezzulo and Cisek, 2016; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Richter et al., 2017; Squire et al., 2013; van Wassenhove et al., 2005; Wyart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to previous work.

claim: Two recent perceptual decision-making studies in macaques found that irrelevant sensory inputs are not filtered out before the integration stage.
source: However, two recent perceptual decision-making studies in macaques found that irrelevant sensory inputs are not filtered out before the integration stage (Mante et al., 2013; Siegel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous macaque studies.

claim: Information about both relevant and irrelevant input dimensions was present in premotor cortex in naive human participants, but irrelevant inputs were weaker than relevant inputs.
source: This showed that information about both relevant and irrelevant input dimensions was present in premotor cortex, but irrelevant inputs were weaker than relevant inputs, consistent with top-down suppression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pre-training data.

claim: Extensive training on over 20,000 trials did not change the input selection mechanisms evident in the MEG recordings.
source: In an attempt to reconcile our findings with those obtained in macaques, we next mirrored NHP training conditions, and our human participants underwent extensive training on over 20,000 trials of the task. However, this did not change the input selection mechanisms evident in the MEG recordings taken afterwards.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the post-training data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Irrelevant inputs were present but still more weakly than relevant inputs when examining information processed in premotor cortex after over-training.
source: Irrelevant inputs were present, but still more weakly than relevant inputs. This was true when examining information processed in premotor cortex, or when decoding from whole-brain activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the post-training data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Twenty-two participants with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorder participated in the study.
source: Twenty-five participants (10 male, 15 female, age range 19–32, mean age 25 ± 0.68) with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorder, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and who fulfilled screening criteria for undergoing MRI and MEG scanning, took part in this study.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: One participant dropped out before completing the experiment and two participants' data sets were too noisy, resulting in a final sample of 22 participants.
source: One participant dropped out before completing the experiment and two participants' data sets were too noisy even after rigorous data clean-up. The final sample thus included 22 participants (10 male, 12 female, age range 19–32, mean age 25 ± 0.74).
evidence: This describes the final participant sample after exclusions.

claim: The study was approved by the University College London Research Ethics Committee.
source: The study was approved by the University College London (UCL) Research Ethics Committee (reference 1825/005) and all participants gave written informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants performed a modified version of a dynamic random-dot-motion decision task where stimuli simultaneously contained information about colour and motion.
source: Participants (n = 22) performed a modified version of a dynamic random-dot-motion (RDM) decision task, in which stimuli simultaneously contained information about colour (red vs. green) and motion (left vs. right, as in Mante et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the experimental task.

claim: A flanker stimulus displayed 150 ms before the RDM stimulus instructed participants about the relevant stimulus dimension.
source: An additional flanker stimulus displayed 150 ms before the RDM stimulus instructed participants about the relevant stimulus dimension: arrows indicated the choice in the current trial was about the dominant motion direction, whereas coloured dots instructed participants to respond based on the dominant colour (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Left PMd was the strongest peak at the whole-brain level for the contrast probing any input or response adaptation.
source: Indeed, left PMd, in a cluster together with left M1, was the strongest peak at the whole-brain level for this contrast (p(FWE)=0.018 cluster-level corrected; left M1: z = 6.10, peak MNI coordinate x=-36, y=-18, z = 48; left PMd: z = 5.02, peak MNI coordinate x=-37, y=-6, z = 55; right PMd: z = 3.11 at x = 37, y = 06, z = 55; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the source localization analysis.

claim: Linear regression coefficients from left premotor cortex demonstrate an early representation of context and switch from approximately 8 ms.
source: Linear regression coefficients from a regression performed on data from left premotor cortex (PMd) demonstrate an early representation of context (motion or colour) and switch (attended dimension same or different from TS) from ~8 ms (sliding window centred on 8 ms contains 150 ms data from [−67,83] ms).
evidence: This is a finding from the time-resolved regression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The representation of inputs emerged from around 108 ms in left premotor cortex.
source: The representation of inputs, as indexed using repetition suppression (RS), emerged from around 108 ms (whether or not the input feature, colour, or motion was repeated).
evidence: This is a finding from the time-resolved regression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The motor response and TS choice direction were processed from 275 ms in left premotor cortex.
source: Finally, the motor response, again indexed using RS (same finger used to respond to adaptation stimulus [AS] and test stimulus [TS] or not), and TS choice direction (left or right, unrelated to RS) were processed from 275 ms.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-resolved regression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Statistical tests showed a significant difference in processing latency for the five regressors.
source: Statistical tests performed on the peaks of the linear regression coefficients obtained for the five regressors showed a significant difference in processing latency (one-way repeated-measures ANOVA: F(4, 84)=128.71, p=5.5154e-35, η2p = 0.86; Figure 2C)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of peak timings.

claim: A pairwise post-hoc test confirmed a significant timing difference with choice input representations preceding response representations.
source: and a pairwise post-hoc test between the two critical regressors, input and response repetition suppression, confirmed a significant timing difference with the choice input representations preceding the response representations (pairwise t-test on peak linear regression coefficients for input [429.5 ± 35 ms; mean ± s.t.d.] and response [531.1 ± 41.6 ms]: t(21)=11.07, p=3.1654e-9, after Bonferroni familywise error correction; Hedges' g = 2.577, 95% CI = [1.8647, 3.4166]; see 'Materials and methods'; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the pairwise comparison of peak timings.

claim: Both relevant and irrelevant inputs were processed significantly from 208 ms in PMd.
source: Comparing the linear regression coefficients capturing the processing of relevant and irrelevant inputs, both indexed using repetition suppression, showed that both were processed significantly from 208 ms
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis comparing relevant and irrelevant input processing shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When the suppressed sensory dimension was relevant to the choice, this had a stronger effect on the signal compared to when it was irrelevant.
source: but importantly, when the suppressed sensory dimension was relevant to the choice at hand, this had a stronger effect on the signal compared to when it was irrelevant (p<0.001 between 375–442 and 675–875 ms; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the comparison of relevant and irrelevant input processing shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Repetition suppression effects were greater for relevant compared to irrelevant sensory information, suggesting prioritized processing of choice-relevant over choice-irrelevant sensory inputs in PMd.
source: In other words, repetition suppression effects were greater for relevant compared to irrelevant sensory information, suggesting prioritized processing of choice-relevant over choice-irrelevant sensory inputs in PMd.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding about relevant vs. irrelevant input processing.

claim: The data show partial but incomplete filtering of irrelevant inputs in PMd.
source: Thus, our data show partial but incomplete filtering of irrelevant inputs in PMd.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the relevant vs. irrelevant input processing data.

claim: Feature selection did not occur solely at the motor output stage of the decision process.
source: Feature selection did not occur solely at the motor output stage of the decision process, nor was irrelevant information entirely filtered out by this stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data about input processing.

claim: Training led to a speeding up of reaction times and higher performance scores.
source: Unsurprisingly, this led to a speeding up of reaction times and higher performance scores (2×2×3 repeated-measures ANOVA with factors context [motion vs. colour], training [pre vs. post], and coherence [70% (AS) vs. 25.6% vs. 12.8%]; effect of training on log-reaction times (RTs): F(1,20)=9.23, p=6.46e-3, η2p = 0.32, mean RT difference 29 ± 10 ms; effect of training on % correct: F(1,20)=36.39, p=6.75e-6, η2p = 0.65, mean difference 4.76 ± 0.8; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis comparing pre- and post-training performance.

claim: The unfolding of the choice computation was evident in signals recorded from PMd after training.
source: Upon completion of the training, we again recorded MEG data during performance of the task in the same way as done in pre-training. As before, the unfolding of the choice computation was evident in signals recorded from PMd (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the post-training MEG analysis.

claim: The difference between processing of relevant and irrelevant inputs was retained after extensive training.
source: Crucially, however, when we repeated the analysis focussing on any differences between the processing of relevant and irrelevant inputs, the difference was retained (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the post-training analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: There was no interaction between input processing and training.
source: There was no interaction between input processing and training (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with factors input [relevant vs. irrelevant] and training [pre vs. post]: all p>0.05 for effect of input x training; Bonferroni correction for familywise error rate; a two-way repeated-measures Bayesian ANOVA provided further evidence in favour of the null hypothesis: the input x training interaction was not part of the winning model at any time point).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of pre- and post-training data.

claim: Peak timings of the majority of regressors occur earlier in the post-compared to the pre-training data.
source: However, peak timings of the majority of regressors occur earlier in the post-compared to the pre-training data, suggesting a faster and possibly more efficient coding of the choice process.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of peak timings pre- and post-training shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Peak timings changed for four out of five regressors following the training.
source: Post-hoc tests confirmed that peak timings changed for four out of five regressors following the training, including the processing of context switches, input adaptation, response adaptation, and choice direction (pairwise t-test between pre vs. post on the peak timings of context: t(21) = 0.18, p=1.00, Hedges' g = 0.046, 95% CI = [−0.481, 0.575]; switch: t(21) = 5.92, p=3.5641e-05, Hedges' g = 1.98, 95% CI = [−0.481, 0.575]; input repetition suppression: t(21) = 5.91, p=3.6398e-05, Hedges' g = 1.57, 95% CI = [0.94, 2.27]; response repetition suppression: t(21) = 12.15, p=2.8914e-10, Hedges' g = 3.08, 95% CI = [2.28, 4.02]; choice: t(21) = 11.09, p=1.5246e-09, Hedges' g = 3.28, 95% CI = [2.35, 4.37]; Bonferroni correction for familywise error rate; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the post-hoc tests on peak timings.

claim: Participants were slower and less accurate when the relevant input had already been processed at the time of the AS and was therefore suppressed at the time of the TS.
source: Consistent with our predictions, participants were slower and less accurate when the relevant input had already been processed at the time of the AS and was therefore suppressed at the time of the TS (RT: t(21)=6.80, p=1.00e-6, Hedges' g = 2.00, 95% CI = [1.18, 2.92]; accuracy: t(21)=-8.65, p=2.28e-8, Hedges' g = −2.55, 95% CI = [−3.60,–1.62]).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis of RT and accuracy.

claim: Participants were less accurate when the motor response was repeated.
source: Similarly, they were less accurate when the motor response was repeated (accuracy; t(21)=-2.28, p=0.03, Hedges' g = −0.67, 95% CI = [−1.33,–0.05]; Figure 5
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis of accuracy.

claim: Neither RTs nor choice accuracies were affected by repetition of the irrelevant sensory feature.
source: However, neither RTs nor choice accuracies were affected by repetition of the irrelevant sensory feature (RT: t(21)=0.13, p=0.90, Hedges' g = 0.04, 95% CI = [−0.57, 0.64]; accuracy: t(21)=0.03, p=0.98, Hedges' g = 0.01, 95% CI = [−0.60, 0.61]).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis showing no effect of irrelevant input repetition.

claim: None of the other a priori regions (V1, V4+V5, mPFC, LIP) showed the transition from processing choice input to processing the motor response observed in PMd.
source: To further show the specificity of our findings, we repeated all key analyses for a few other a priori regions known to be implicated in visual feature selection and choice: primary visual cortex (V1), higher-order visual cortices (V4 and V5), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and lateral intraparietal area (LIP). None of these regions showed the transition from processing choice input to processing the motor response observed in PMd (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for all regions; Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for a priori regions).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of other brain regions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Decoding across all parcels showed weaker decoding of irrelevant compared to relevant inputs.
source: Consistent with earlier analyses, decoding across all parcels showed weaker decoding of irrelevant compared to relevant inputs (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain decoding analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was significant decoding of irrelevant inputs from 455 to 708.3 ms post-TS.
source: There was some significant decoding of irrelevant inputs (p<0.001 from 455 to 708.3 ms post-TS) but it was again less extended in time and weaker compared to the decoding of relevant inputs (p<0.001 from 201.7 to 961.7 ms post-TS; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain decoding analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was no difference between the data acquired pre- vs. post-training in whole-brain decoding apart from differences in peak timing.
source: There was again no difference between the data acquired pre- vs. post-training (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with factors input [relevant vs. irrelevant] and training [pre vs. post]: all p>0.5; minimum p=0.52, F(1,21) = 5.49, η2p = 0.21, for effect of training; Bonferroni correction for familywise error rate; a two-way repeated-measures Bayesian ANOVA provided further evidence in favour of the null hypothesis: the input x training interaction was not part of the winning model at any time point) apart from differences in peak timing (Figure 6B
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the whole-brain decoding analysis.

claim: Non-invasively recorded MEG activity can be used to track a choice process on a millisecond timescale.
source: Here we have shown that non-invasively recorded MEG activity can be used to track a choice process on a millisecond timescale.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: As decisions unfolded, MEG activity in premotor cortex transitioned from processing sensory inputs to processing the motor response.
source: As decisions unfolded, MEG activity in premotor cortex transitioned from processing sensory inputs to processing the motor response.
evidence: This is a summary of a main finding of the study.

claim: In human premotor cortex, sensory inputs irrelevant to the current choice were processed more weakly compared to relevant choice inputs.
source: We found that in human premotor cortex, sensory inputs irrelevant to the current choice were processed more weakly compared to relevant choice inputs.
evidence: This is a summary of a main finding of the study.

claim: This partial filtering of irrelevant choice features was observed even after extensive over-training and when considering activity present across the brain.
source: This partial filtering of irrelevant choice features was observed even after extensive over-training and when considering activity present across the brain.
evidence: This is a summary of a main finding of the study.

claim: Studying neural population responses has provided crucial insights into the evolution of choice.
source: It has provided crucial insights, for example, into the evolution of choice (Harvey et al., 2012; Hunt et al., 2018; Mante et al., 2013; Morcos and Harvey, 2016; Raposo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Studying neural population responses has provided crucial insights into movement preparation and execution.
source: movement preparation and execution (Churchland et al., 2012; Kaufman et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Studying neural population responses has provided crucial insights into the mechanisms underlying working memory.
source: and the mechanisms underlying working memory (Murray et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Repetition suppression has been exploited for understanding a wide range of cognitive processes with both fMRI and MEG/EEG.
source: While this insight has been exploited for understanding a wide range of cognitive processes, with both fMRI (Barron et al., 2013; Barron et al., 2016b; Chong et al., 2008; Doeller et al., 2010; Garvert et al., 2017; Garvert et al., 2015; Jenkins et al., 2008; Klein-Flügge et al., 2019; Klein-Flügge et al., 2013; Piazza et al., 2007) and MEG/EEG (Fritsche et al., 2020; Henson, 2016; Henson et al., 2004; Todorovic and de Lange, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to previous work.

claim: The obtained trajectories are comparable to population traces from invasive recordings in NHPs in that they show a progression from processing of choice inputs to processing of the motor response.
source: The obtained trajectories are comparable to population traces from invasive recordings in NHPs (Figures 3 and 4; Mante et al., 2013) in that they show a progression from a processing of choice inputs to a processing of the motor response.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous NHP work, supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In Mante et al., 2013, the influence of input returned to baseline before choice execution because monkeys were only allowed to indicate a response after a delay, once the motion stimulus had been turned off.
source: However, in Mante et al., 2013, the influence of input returned to baseline before choice execution. This may be because monkeys were only allowed to indicate a response after a delay, once the motion stimulus had been turned off.
evidence: This is an interpretation of differences between the current study and previous NHP work.

claim: In human choice trajectories, input representations started to return to baseline just before the time of response but did not fully return to zero by the time participants responded.
source: By contrast, we allowed participants to respond at any time while the stimulus was presented, and thus the trial could end before input processing returned to zero. Indeed, in our human choice trajectories, input representations started to return to baseline just before the time of response but did not fully return to zero by the time participants responded.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of choice trajectories.

claim: The neural mechanisms underlying repetition suppression are not fully understood to date.
source: The neural mechanisms underlying repetition suppression are not fully understood to date.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Hypothesized mechanisms for repetition suppression include neuronal sharpening, fatigue, and facilitation, with current evidence favouring the fatigue model.
source: Hypothesized mechanisms include neuronal sharpening, fatigue, and facilitation, with current evidence favouring the fatigue model according to which suppression is caused by attenuated synaptic inputs (Barron et al., 2016b; Grill-Spector et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on repetition suppression mechanisms.

claim: The authors observe adaptation of not just sensory inputs but also the motor response, and of not just attended but also unattended sensory inputs.
source: However, we observe adaptation of not just sensory inputs but also the motor response, and of not just attended but also unattended sensory inputs (Larsson and Smith, 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the study that supports an interpretation as suppression rather than prediction error.

claim: The key effects reported all come from within the same region, eliminating inter-regional differences in neural dynamics as a possible explanation for timing differences.
source: Importantly, however, the key effects reported here all come from within the same region. This eliminates inter-regional differences in neural dynamics as a possible explanation for the timing differences we observed between sensory and motor suppression effects.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the timing differences observed.

claim: The authors report absolute linear regression coefficients throughout because the arbitrary nature of the orientation of the MEG dipoles means they cannot be certain about whether feature repetition causes a suppression or enhancement in the underlying neural signal.
source: Ultimately, the arbitrary nature of the orientation of the MEG dipoles fitted means that we cannot be certain about whether feature repetition causes a suppression or enhancement in the underlying neural signal. For that reason, we report absolute linear regression coefficients throughout.
evidence: This explains a methodological choice in the analysis.

claim: Single-unit studies provide strong and consistent evidence for a suppression, rather than enhancement, of neural responses after repeated exposure to a sensory feature.
source: However, single-unit studies provide strong and consistent evidence for a suppression, rather than enhancement, of neural responses after repeated exposure to a sensory feature (Barron et al., 2016b; Grill-Spector et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous single-unit studies.

claim: Behavioral results are consistent with the interpretation that inputs are suppressed as a result of repeated exposure to a feature.
source: Our behavioural results are consistent with the interpretation that inputs are suppressed as a result of repeated exposure to a feature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Repetition of the relevant sensory feature or response, but not the irrelevant sensory feature, reduced choice accuracies.
source: Repetition of the relevant sensory feature or response, but not the irrelevant sensory feature, reduced choice accuracies
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Repetition of relevant, but not irrelevant, sensory features slowed RTs.
source: and repetition of relevant, but not irrelevant, sensory features slowed RTs.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A substantial body of evidence in human and non-human primates has shown that selection of relevant sensory features occurs through top-down modulations from prefrontal and parietal regions onto early sensory regions.
source: A substantial body of evidence both in human and non-human primates has shown that selection of relevant sensory features occurs through top-down modulations from prefrontal and parietal regions onto early sensory regions (Buschman and Miller, 2007; de Lange et al., 2010; Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Everling et al., 2002; Friston, 2005; Friston and Kiebel, 2009; Kok et al., 2016; Michalareas et al., 2016; Moore and Zirnsak, 2017; Noudoost et al., 2010; Pezzulo and Cisek, 2016; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Richter et al., 2017; Squire et al., 2013; Summerfield et al., 2014; van Wassenhove et al., 2005; Wyart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to previous work.

source: Indeed, in a task with only relevant features, training changes neuronal responses responsible for interpreting sensory evidence, but not those processing the sensory evidence itself (Law and Gold, 2010; Law and Gold, 2008).

claim: The only difference identified between naive and extensively over-trained participants was a shift in peak timings.
source: To our surprise, the only difference identified between naive and extensively over-trained participants was a shift in peak timings (Figures 4 and 5).

Consistent with predictive coding principles and theories of top-down control, the processing of irrelevant inputs was diminished
